newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Lebed sacking not a "turning point".
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Lebed sacking not a "turning point".

text.p: The United States said on Thursday the sacking of President Boris Yeltsin's security chief Alexander Lebed did not appear to be "a fundamental turning point" and that the Russian government was stable.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said it was not appropriate for Washington to comment on what was an internal decision, but added: "I don't think the American public needs to worry that this is some fundamental turning point."

Burns said: "This is dramatic. It's important. We're not exactly sure where it's going to lead in the future but the (U.S.-Russian) relationship is stable and this is what matters ultimately to the American people."
Speaking at a regular State Department briefing, Burns said: "The Russian government is stable, led by President Yeltsin...".
Burns and White House spokesman Mike McCurry, who is travelling with President Bill Clinton in California, said Yeltsin was acting within his constitutional powers.

McCurry said Clinton had been briefed on the situation by national security aides, adding: "The (U.S.) embassy reports there is no unusual activity in Moscow in response to President Yeltsin's announcement that we're aware of."

Yeltsin fired Lebed on Thursday after just four months in office, saying he could no longer tolerate what Yeltsin termed Lebed's lack of team spirit and obvious ambition to become Russia's next leader.
The United States has had mixed feelings about Lebed, a reserve general who scored a strong 15 percent in the first round of Russia's presidential election last June.

Washington welcomed Lebed's success in negotiating an end to fighting in Chechnya, and also praised comments he made during a visit to Brussels this month which appeared to take a flexible view of NATO expansion.
But U.S. officials have also seen him as something of a loose cannon and have condemned comments he made which they said were hostile to religious groups, including Jews and Roman Catholics.
Clinton has invested much political capital in maintaining good relations with Russia as the country struggles through economic and social upheavals following the collapse of the Soviet Union.

"Russia has been for five years in a period of historic transition. The trends are positive in Russia," Burns said, noting a spread of democracy through the country and signs of recovery from the economic slump of the early 1990s.
"We just want to keep those trends going," he said.

Burns said U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, who is visiting Russia, was told about Lebed's dismissal "a couple of minutes" before Yeltsin's announcement. Perry had been due to meet Lebed about that time and put the meeting off.

He said the Clinton administration was confident it could work with Yeltsin's government, including securing ratification of the Start II nuclear weapons treaty which is the subject of Perry's trip, adding: "We're not going to stop now because of a little political turmoil in Moscow."
In Moscow, Perry said Lebed's sacking would not change the deepening security relationship between Washington and Moscow.

"The relationship between Mr Lebed and U.S. officials never really had a chance to develop, and so I don't see any fundamental change in the U.S.-Russian relationship in terms of this announcement," Perry told reporters.
